title: The Decoy Effect

scenes.text: Why does the *medium* popcorn always win?
scenes.vo: Ever notice you always end up buying the medium popcorn? That's not an accident.
Imagine a cinema sells small popcorn for 150 rupees and large for 300. Most people pick small.
Now they add a medium for 270. Suddenly the large looks like a steal. It's only 30 more.

scenes.text:
The medium isn't meant to sell.
It's a *decoy*.
scenes.vo: The medium was never meant to sell. It's a decoy, there to make the large look like a bargain.

scenes.text:
The Economist ad:
Web $59 · Print $125
Web + Print $125
scenes.vo: Dan Ariely tested this with an Economist ad. Web only, 59 dollars. Print only, 125. Print plus web, also 125.

scenes.text:
With the decoy:
*84%* chose Web + Print
scenes.vo: With the useless print-only option on the menu, 84 percent chose the combo.
Remove the decoy, and only 32 percent did.

scenes.text: Ask yourself: would I pick this if the middle option *didn't exist*?
scenes.vo: So next time, ask yourself: would I still pick this if the middle option didn't exist?

caption:
That medium popcorn isn't there for you to buy. 🍿 It's there to make the large look cheap. This is the decoy effect, and it's on almost every menu, pricing page and subscription plan you see.

Spotted a decoy recently? Drop it in the comments 👇
source: Ariely, D. (2008). Predictably Irrational, ch. 1 (The Economist subscription experiment); Huber, Payne & Puto (1982), Journal of Consumer Research.
